cards.headline: Where your shares actually live.
cards.body: You do not hold shares directly — they sit in a **brokerage account** you open with a broker. Which type of account you use quietly changes how much of your return you keep.

cards.headline: Two flavours of account.
cards.body: A **taxable brokerage** account is flexible: invest and withdraw anytime, but you owe tax on gains. **Retirement accounts** like an IRA or 401(k) trade some of that access for large tax advantages.
Three costs quietly eat into returns. None feels big on its own; together, over decades, they add up.

cards.title: What a 1% fee costs
cards.caption: Same $10,000 over 30 years. Earning **7%** versus **6%** — a single 1% fee — leaves a strikingly different final balance. Fees compound against you.

cards.headline: Sell for a profit, and tax appears.
cards.body: In a **taxable** account, selling a stock for more than you paid creates a **capital gain** — and you owe tax on it. Hold longer than a year and the rate is usually lower.

cards.prompt: You sell a stock at a profit after holding it 13 months. Which tax usually applies?
cards.explanation: Held **longer than one year**, the gain is **long-term**, usually taxed more gently than a short-term gain. Thirteen months clears that one-year bar.

cards.headline: Accounts that shelter growth.
cards.body: **Tax-advantaged** accounts are the biggest lever most people have. A traditional IRA or 401(k) defers tax until you withdraw; a **Roth** is funded with already-taxed money and then grows tax-free.
Holding a stock longer than [[1]] usually qualifies the gain for the lower long-term rate.
cards.explanation: In the U.S., a gain becomes **long-term** once you have held for more than a year — and long-term gains are usually taxed more gently than short-term ones.

cards.headline: The honest caveat.
cards.body: Tax rules vary by country and by your own situation, and they change. This teaches the **shape** of how accounts, fees, and taxes work — not your specific bill. For that, ask a professional.

cards.summary: The account you choose, the fees you pay, and the tax on your gains quietly decide how much you actually keep.
bullets: Taxable accounts are flexible; retirement accounts save tax.
Small fees compound into a large drag over decades.
Held over a year, gains usually get the lower long-term rate.

cards.insight: Your return is what you earn. What you keep is that minus fees and taxes — and those are the parts you can most control.
